chapters.title: CHAPTER 1: THE CLOUD HAS AN ADDRESS

lines.say: In a quiet neighbourhood outside Manassas, Virginia, there's a sound that never stops.
lines.show: White paper. A row of houses fades in, drawn in ink. A thin waveform starts pulsing.

lines.say: Not a siren. Not traffic. A hum. Day and night.
lines.show: The waveform steadies into a constant line. A clock spins; the hum line never breaks.

lines.say: It comes from the building across the road. A building with no windows, no sign, and almost no people.
lines.show: A huge grey box slides in from the right and dwarfs the houses.

lines.say: It's a data centre. And it's one of the most boring buildings ever designed.
lines.show: Label: "Data centre." The box sits there, doing nothing.

lines.say: So here's the puzzle.
lines.show: Beat.

lines.say: In the first three months of 2026, local opposition blocked or delayed about 130 billion dollars of these buildings across the US.
lines.show: A counter rolls up to $130B. Pins drop across a US map. Source: Data Center Watch.

lines.say: Between April and June, another 68 billion.
lines.show: The counter adds $68B.

lines.say: There are now more than 800 groups fighting them, in every state except Hawaii.
lines.show: The map fills with dots. Hawaii stays empty and gets a small circle.

lines.say: Why would anyone get this angry at a box full of computers?
lines.show: Title card: **WHY PEOPLE HATE DATA CENTRES**

lines.say: To understand the anger, we have to start with what's inside.
lines.show: Chapter card 1.

lines.say: Every time you stream a show, send a photo, or ask an AI a question, a computer somewhere does the work.
lines.show: A phone at the centre. Icons fly out along lines toward the edge of the frame.

lines.say: We call that place "the cloud." But the cloud isn't in the sky.
lines.show: A soft cloud drawing floats up, then drops and lands as a grey box.

lines.say: It's in buildings like this one. Rows and rows of servers, stacked in racks, running every second of every day.
lines.show: Cutaway of the box: racks slide in from left and right, and tiny status lights blink.

lines.say: And many of them sit in one place.
lines.show: A map zooms in on Northern Virginia.

lines.say: Look at this. Loudoun County, Virginia. Locals call it Data Center Alley.
lines.show: Satellite-style map. Hundreds of grey rectangles appear one after another.

lines.say: It has one of the biggest concentrations of data centres on Earth.
lines.show: The rectangles keep appearing until the county is crowded.

lines.say: Why here? It's an accident of history.
lines.show: A question mark drawn in ink over the county.

lines.say: In the early 1990s, one of the internet's first big exchange points, a place where networks swap traffic, opened just down the road. It was called MAE-East.
lines.show: A small building with many cables converging on it. Label: "MAE-East, 1992".

lines.say: AOL moved its headquarters to Ashburn in 1996. Fibre optic cable followed.
lines.show: An AOL-era beige computer slides in. Glowing fibre lines spread across the map.

lines.say: And once the cables were there, every new data centre wanted to be close to them.
lines.show: New boxes snap onto the fibre lines like beads on a string.

lines.say: Close to the cables meant faster connections. So they kept clustering.
lines.show: The beads multiply into a dense cluster.

lines.say: For years, nobody really noticed them. They were quiet neighbours.
lines.show: The rectangles fade to a pale grey and sit in the background.

lines.say: Then AI changed the maths.
lines.show: Hard cut. An AI chip slides in, glowing in the accent colour.

lines.say: Training and running AI models takes enormous amounts of computing, and that takes enormous amounts of electricity.
lines.show: The chip multiplies into a grid of chips. A power meter needle swings up.

lines.say: In 2023, data centres used about 4.4 percent of all electricity in the United States.
lines.show: Bar chart: a small bar labelled 4.4%. Source: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

lines.say: By 2028, the government's own researchers think it could be as much as 12 percent.
lines.show: The bar grows to a range between 6.7% and 12%.

lines.say: Worldwide, the International Energy Agency expects data centre electricity use to roughly double by 2030.
lines.show: A globe with a rising line. Source: IEA.

lines.say: A single new AI campus can now need as much power as a small city.
lines.show: A glowing box next to a city skyline of equal size.

lines.say: That's the shift. These buildings went from quiet neighbours to some of the biggest customers on the grid.
lines.show: The grey box grows until it rivals the town beside it.

lines.say: And when something that big plugs into the grid, everyone connected to it feels it.
lines.show: Cables run from the box to many small houses.

lines.say: Which brings us to the first reason people are angry. The bill.
lines.show: A power bill envelope drops onto the paper.

lines.say: Your electricity doesn't just come from a power plant. It comes from a shared system called the grid.
lines.show: Chapter card 2. A network diagram of plants, lines and homes.

lines.say: And the grid has to be ready for the busiest moment of the year, not the average day.
lines.show: A line chart with a peak. A dashed "must be ready" line sits above it.

lines.say: In the eastern US, a grid operator called PJM keeps that promise for about 65 million people.
lines.show: The PJM region highlighted across 13 states. "65 million people."

lines.say: Once a year, it holds an auction to pay power plants to be available when needed.
lines.show: An auction gavel. Power plant icons line up with price tags.

lines.say: Think of it like reserving seats for a concert that might sell out.
lines.show: Simple theatre seats. Some fill with "reserved" tags.

lines.say: When lots of new people want seats, the price of reserving one goes up.
lines.show: New data centre icons walk in. Price tags jump.

lines.say: And the new arrivals want a lot of seats. Tech companies are planning data centres that each need hundreds of megawatts.
lines.show: One data centre icon takes a whole row of seats.

lines.say: Look at what happened.
lines.show: Beat.

lines.say: For 2024 to 2025, a megawatt of capacity cost about 29 dollars a day.
lines.show: A bar at $28.92/MW-day. Source: PJM.

lines.say: The next year: about 270 dollars. Almost ten times more.
lines.show: The bar shoots up to $269.92.

lines.say: Then: 329 dollars, the maximum allowed.
lines.show: The bar hits a red "price cap" line.

lines.say: The grid's independent market monitor found data centres were responsible for most of that jump, about 63 percent of the increase in one auction.
lines.show: A pie chart: 63% in the accent colour. Source: Monitoring Analytics via IEEFA.

lines.say: And who pays for capacity? Everyone on the grid. Including you.
lines.show: The cost flows down from the auction into every house icon.

lines.say: Across the region, household supply rates rose by between 5 and 44 percent, depending on the utility.
lines.show: A range bar from 5% to 44%, with utility names as small labels.

lines.say: Then there are the wires. New power lines and substations to reach these campuses cost billions, and those costs often get spread across all customers.
lines.show: Transmission towers march across the map toward the data centres.

lines.say: Utilities and data centre companies argue the big customers pay their fair share, and some states now make them sign special contracts to prove it.
lines.show: A contract slides in with a pen, captioned "large-load tariffs".

lines.say: But from a kitchen table, it looks simple.
lines.show: A kitchen table with a bill on it.

lines.say: My bill went up. The building down the road is new.
lines.show: The bill and the grey box sit side by side on the paper.

lines.say: And nobody asked me.
lines.show: Text: "nobody asked me."

lines.say: That feeling, of paying for something you didn't choose, shows up again and again.
lines.show: The words fade into a dotted line that leads to the next scene.

lines.say: Including in the next thing these buildings need.
lines.show: A water drop falls and splashes.

lines.say: Computers get hot. Tens of thousands of chips, packed together, make a lot of heat.
lines.show: Chapter card 3. A heat map glows over the server racks.

lines.say: One of the cheapest ways to cool them is to evaporate water, like sweat on skin.
lines.show: A cooling tower diagram. Water droplets rise and vanish.

lines.say: Most of that water doesn't come back. It turns into vapour and leaves.
lines.show: Arrows: water in, a big arrow up as vapour, a small arrow out. Label: "around 80% evaporates".

lines.say: A typical data centre can use around 300,000 gallons a day. Roughly what a thousand homes use.
lines.show: Water bottles fill a grid. 1 building equals 1,000 houses.

lines.say: The biggest can use millions.
lines.show: The grid of houses keeps expanding.

lines.say: Now picture that in a place that's already short of water.
lines.show: The map shifts to the desert Southwest, in dry browns.

lines.say: In 2025, a huge project codenamed "Project Blue" came to Tucson, Arizona.
lines.show: A folder stamped "PROJECT BLUE".

lines.say: Residents packed city meetings. And Tucson's council voted to walk away from it.
lines.show: A packed council chamber drawn in simple shapes. A vote tally.

lines.say: In Georgia, near a Meta data centre, some neighbours say their wells started failing after construction began.
lines.show: A well bucket comes up dry. The Meta building is shown as a generic grey box.

lines.say: Meta says its own studies found no link.
lines.show: A caption card: "Meta: no link found in its studies."

lines.say: But you can see why people are suspicious.
lines.show: Beat.

lines.say: Newer permits there allow for up to six million gallons a day.
lines.show: A gauge rises to "6M gallons/day (permit)".

lines.say: To be fair, many newer designs use closed-loop cooling that barely consumes any water at all.
lines.show: A clean closed-loop diagram, with water circling and not escaping.

lines.say: But that uses more electricity instead. So the problem moves back to the grid.
lines.show: The loop's arrow points to the power meter from Chapter 2.

lines.say: Power or water. Every data centre makes a trade.
lines.show: A balance scale with a lightning bolt on one side and a drop on the other.

lines.say: And the neighbours pay for either side.
lines.show: The scale tips onto a row of houses.

lines.say: Remember that hum?
lines.show: Chapter card 4. The waveform from the cold open returns.

lines.say: In the Great Oak neighbourhood of Manassas, residents said a nearby Amazon Web Services campus filled their evenings with a constant, high-pitched whir.
lines.show: The house outline, with a speaker icon pulsing from the grey box.

lines.say: Fans and chillers on the roof run all the time. The sound doesn't stop at night.
lines.show: Roof fans spin. The sky turns to night; the waveform keeps going.

lines.say: Counties in Virginia have been rewriting their noise rules just to keep up.
lines.show: A rulebook page flips, with new lines underlined.

lines.say: Then there's the air.
lines.show: Clear sky turns to a light grey haze.

lines.say: In South Memphis, Elon Musk's company xAI built a giant AI supercomputer called Colossus in a matter of months.
lines.show: The Memphis skyline. A box rises fast with a speed-line blur.

lines.say: To power it quickly, it brought in gas turbines, dozens of them.
lines.show: Turbine icons appear one by one.

lines.say: The Southern Environmental Law Center counted 35 running without permits.
lines.show: A counter to 35. Each turbine gets a small red "no permit" tag. Source: SELC.

lines.say: The nearest neighbourhood, Boxtown, is a historically Black community that already lived with heavy industry.
lines.show: A small neighbourhood drawing beside the factory icons.

lines.say: Local officials later granted permits for 15 turbines. Residents and civil rights groups are still fighting.
lines.show: A permit document with "15" on it. Protest sign shapes.

lines.say: And then there's land.
lines.show: The haze clears to fields.

lines.say: In Prince William County, Virginia, a plan called the Digital Gateway would have covered about 2,100 acres with data centres.
lines.show: A map outline fills with grey across green fields.

lines.say: Right next to a Civil War battlefield.
lines.show: A battlefield marker next to the grey area.

lines.say: It would have been one of the largest data centre campuses in the world.
lines.show: Scale comparison against Data Center Alley.

lines.say: Residents sued. A court voided the rezoning, and the developer gave up its appeal.
lines.show: A gavel. The grey area peels away and the fields return.

lines.say: Noise. Air. Land. None of these is new. Factories and highways have caused all of them.
lines.show: Three icons in a row: ear, cloud, tree. Old factory and highway drawings appear behind them.

lines.say: The difference is that those things usually came with lots of jobs.
lines.show: A factory with many little worker figures.

lines.say: Which raises the obvious question.
lines.show: Beat.

lines.say: What does a town actually get in return?
lines.show: A handshake that pauses before it closes.

lines.say: Data centres cost a fortune to build. Hundreds of millions of dollars, sometimes billions.
lines.show: Chapter card 5. A stack of money builds up.

lines.say: But once they're running, they need surprisingly few people.
lines.show: The money stack stays. Little worker figures appear, only a handful.

lines.say: Building one does create jobs: hundreds, sometimes thousands, of construction workers. But those jobs end when the building is finished.
lines.show: Hard hats fill the site, then walk off one by one.

lines.say: Virginia's own auditors found a typical large data centre employs about 50 full-time workers, and around half of them are contractors.
lines.show: 50 figures, half in outline. Source: JLARC.

lines.say: Meanwhile, many states hand them big tax breaks to win them.
lines.show: Coins slide back from a state building to the box.

lines.say: Virginia's sales tax exemption for data centre equipment cost state and local governments about 1.9 billion dollars in 2025.
lines.show: A counter to $1.9B. Source: Good Jobs First.

lines.say: One watchdog group worked it out at more than a million dollars for every new job.
lines.show: "$1.2M per job", big, in the accent colour.

lines.say: But here's the other side, and it matters.
lines.show: Beat. The paper flips.

lines.say: Virginia's own study found the exemption was one of the state's best-performing incentives, producing about six dollars of labour income for every dollar given up.
lines.show: A $1 coin turns into $6.10. Source: JLARC.

lines.say: And look at Loudoun County, Data Center Alley itself.
lines.show: The Chapter 1 map returns.

lines.say: Data centres bring in about 1.3 billion dollars a year in local taxes, around 38 percent of the county's general fund.
lines.show: A pie chart, 38% in the accent colour. Source: Loudoun County.

lines.say: That money helped cut the homeowner property tax rate every year for a decade.
lines.show: A line falling from $1.145 to $0.805 per $100.

lines.say: So data centres can be a great deal. For the right place.
lines.show: A green check over Loudoun.

lines.say: The catch is that the benefits and the costs often don't land in the same place.
lines.show: The map splits in two: money flows to one county, power lines and costs spread to many.

lines.say: The tax money goes to one county. The power lines, the higher capacity prices, the water, spread out to everyone else.
lines.show: Arrows spread across the whole PJM map.

lines.say: And that mismatch is the heart of this story.
lines.show: The arrows freeze.

lines.say: Look back at every fight in this video, and there's a pattern.
lines.show: Chapter card 6. The small scenes from the video appear as cards.

lines.say: The benefits are global and invisible. Faster apps, smarter AI, profits for some of the biggest companies in the world.
lines.show: One side of the paper: a globe, app icons, stock arrows, all small and far away.

lines.say: The costs are local and very visible. A hum. A bill. A dry well. A field that's gone.
lines.show: The other side: the hum, bill, well and field, big and close.

lines.say: And often, residents find out late. Projects arrive with code names, like Project Blue, and details come after the deal is shaped.
lines.show: Folders with code names slide onto a table.

lines.say: That's why this fight doesn't split neatly between left and right.
lines.show: A US map colouring both red and blue counties in the accent colour.

lines.say: Rural conservatives worried about land and taxes are standing next to environmentalists worried about water and gas.
lines.show: Two groups of figures standing together.

lines.say: And they're winning more often. Around 30 states have now passed rules on where data centres can go and what they can use.
lines.show: State outlines light up one by one.

lines.say: Some towns have simply hit pause. Near Detroit, a utility authority voted to stop new water and sewer service to data centres for a year.
lines.show: A pause symbol over Ypsilanti, Michigan.

lines.say: Meanwhile, the industry keeps planning to build more, and faster, because the demand for computing isn't slowing down.
lines.show: The investment line keeps rising at the top of the frame.

lines.say: So this isn't really a fight about whether data centres should exist.
lines.show: Beat.

lines.say: The phone in your pocket depends on them. So does almost everything online.
lines.show: The phone from Chapter 1 returns, with its lines running to the boxes.

lines.say: It's a fight about who pays, and who gets a say.
lines.show: "who pays" and "who decides" as two big lines.

lines.say: So is there a version of this that neighbours wouldn't hate?
lines.show: Chapter card 7. The house and the box sit side by side.

lines.say: Some places are already trying.
lines.show: A world map. Pins appear.

lines.say: Start with the bill. In Ohio, regulators approved a rule for the biggest new data centres.
lines.show: Ohio highlighted. A tariff document.

lines.say: They must pay for at least 85 percent of the power they reserve, for up to 12 years, even if they don't use it.
lines.show: A gauge fixed at 85%. A 12-year timeline. Source: PUCO / AEP Ohio.

lines.say: The idea is simple. If you ask the grid to build for you, you pay for it, not your neighbours.
lines.show: Arrows of cost now flow back into the box instead of the houses.

lines.say: Then there's the heat. All that warmth the cooling systems throw away could heat homes instead.
lines.show: Heat waves rise from the box, then bend toward the houses.

lines.say: In Denmark, Meta's data centre in Odense sends its waste heat into the city's heating network, for up to 11,000 homes.
lines.show: Denmark outline. Warm pipes run into 11,000 dots.

lines.say: In Finland, Microsoft and the energy company Fortum are building a system to supply about 40 percent of the district heating for around 250,000 people.
lines.show: Finland outline. A heating gauge at 40%.

lines.say: Other fixes are less glamorous. Closed-loop cooling to save water. Real noise limits. Building next to new power instead of plugging into an already stretched grid.
lines.show: Three quick icons with checkmarks.

lines.say: And maybe the biggest one: telling people early. Before the land is bought. Before the deal is done.
lines.show: The code-name folders open, and the documents slide onto the town hall table.

lines.say: None of this makes a data centre invisible.
lines.show: Beat.

lines.say: But it changes the question from "Why is this being done to us?" to "What do we get, and what does it cost?"
lines.show: The two questions appear as ink lines, one crossed out.

lines.say: For years, the internet felt weightless. Something that lived nowhere.
lines.show: The cloud drawing floats up again.

lines.say: But it turns out the cloud has an address.
lines.show: The cloud drops and lands as the grey box across from the house.

lines.say: It uses power, and water, and land. It makes noise.
lines.show: Icons orbit the box: bolt, drop, tree, waveform.

lines.say: And more and more, it's somebody's neighbour.
lines.show: The hum fades. The house light turns on. Hold.

lines.say: The question is whether that neighbour gets to have a say.
lines.show: End card with sources. Credits: "Research: Data Center Watch, LBNL, IEA, PJM, IEEFA, JLARC, Good Jobs First, Loudoun County, SELC."
